description: The PowerShell tool ran the sweeps the Bash tool walls, and saw none of them (DEF-824, DEF-822, and the native-rm sibling filed from the lane's own drive, 2026-09-16). pwsh's alias table is per platform: on macOS and Linux `rm`, `rmdir`, `ls` and `find` resolve to the native binaries (`ri`, `del`, `rd`, `gci`, `dir` stay aliases; on Windows `rm` is Remove-Item), so on a POSIX host routed through the PowerShell tool `find . -delete` and `rm -rf ~` are the real delete -- and the tool had no find arm at all, the two hard records and the soft tier spelled `-Recurse` and `-Force` in full so `ri -r -fo C:\` and `rm -rf ~` drew nothing, a rootless enumerator (`gci -Recurse | ri -r -fo`; Get-ChildItem defaults to `.` as find does) yielded no operand to any tier, and nothing judged a pipeline's root. Driven on pwsh 7.6.5 before the fix: `find . -delete`, `gci -Recurse | ri -r -fo`, `gci | ri -r -fo` and the bash cluster each wiped a throwaway while `_ps_dangerous_reason` answered None to every one. Fix: the recurse and force switches by every spelling that runs (`_PS_RECURSE_SWITCH`, `_PS_FORCE_SWITCH`: the unambiguous cmdlet prefixes, the long forms, the /bin/rm clusters with bash's own rule that an `i` after the last `f` cancels force) composed into the two records and the soft-tier regex, the switch tokenizer reading a cluster as a switch; a `_PS_CMD_POS`-anchored find head sharing the Bash arm's span reader, so both tools keep one reading of what a find takes and what narrows it; an enumerator reader giving the pipeline its roots (the current location when it names none) and reading -Include, -Filter, the positional filter or a wildcard root as narrowing; one PowerShell sweep classifier (`has_catastrophic_ps_sweep`) judging every un-narrowed sweep -- a find with a delete action, a pipeline whose remove verb recurses or whose enumeration is files-only -- from the statement's directory through the Set-Location chain, refused with `CATASTROPHIC_PS_SWEEP` ahead of the maintenance gate; the three rungs taking the pipeline's roots for an operand-less remove verb fed by the pipe; the speed bump's PowerShell branch bumping an un-narrowed sweep root off the roster once. A variable in a root is the wall by this tool's own rule (the Remove-Item tier's). The attempts vary along HEAD (find, the enumerator pipeline, the abbreviated cmdlet, the native rm), ROOT SPELLING and WHAT NARROWS, because a corpus flat along any of those axes would have reported the wall on one spelling and missed the rest.
